title: Metadata & File Signatures 🕵️
description: Master MAC times and magic bytes – the hidden clues that reveal when and what a file really is.

slides.title: The Timestamps That Tell Tales ⏰
slides.content:
# MAC Times

Every file has timestamps – collectively called **MAC times** (or MACB):

- **M**odified: Last time file content changed.
- **A**ccessed: Last time file was read (often disabled for performance).
- **C**hanged (or Created): Metadata change or file birth.
- **B**irth (on some file systems): Original creation time.

These timestamps are crucial for timeline reconstruction.

quizData.question: Which timestamp is updated when a file's permissions are changed?
quizData.explanation: On many systems (like Unix), ctime updates when file metadata (permissions, owner) changes, not just content.

slides.title: Timestamps on Different File Systems 🖥️
slides.content:
- **NTFS**: Stores four timestamps in $STANDARD_INFORMATION and $FILE_NAME attributes. $SI times can be modified by user, $FN times are more accurate (set by kernel).
- **FAT**: Only modified date/time, and accessed date (no creation time in older FAT; FAT32 has create date/time).
- **ext4**: Stores atime, mtime, ctime, and crtime (birth time).

Always note that timestamps can be manipulated (timestomping) – don't treat them as absolute truth.

slides.title: View Timestamps with stat
slides.content: On Linux, `stat` shows all timestamps for a file.

quizData.question: File timestamps can never be altered intentionally.
quizData.explanation: Tools exist to modify timestamps (timestomping) to mislead investigators. That's why correlation with other sources is essential.

slides.title: File Signatures (Magic Bytes) 🪄
slides.content:
## Identity Beyond Extension

A file's true type is determined by its **magic bytes** – a specific sequence at the beginning of the file.

| File Type | Hex Signature |
|-----------|---------------|
| JPEG      | FF D8 FF E0   |
| PNG       | 89 50 4E 47   |
| PDF       | 25 50 44 46   |
| ZIP       | 50 4B 03 04   |
| EXE       | 4D 5A         |

Renaming a .exe to .docx doesn't change its magic bytes. Forensic tools check the header to identify true file types, even if extension is missing.

slides.title: Check Signature with file Command
slides.content: Linux's `file` command uses the magic database to identify file types.
slides.codeSnippet:
file --mime-type unknown_file
# Output: application/pdf (even if renamed to .txt)

quizData.question: The magic bytes for a ZIP file are ___.
quizData.explanation: ZIP files start with 50 4B 03 04, but the first two bytes 'PK' (50 4B) are the signature.

slides.title: ⚠️ Mismatched Extensions = Suspicious
slides.content: A .jpg file with a PDF header is often a sign of data hiding or malware. Always verify file signatures during examination.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use a Custom Signature File

Tools like **TrID** or **Autopsy** can scan for thousands of signatures. But you can also create your own for proprietary file types.
